reads: from our window we could command a view of the avenue gate, and of the inhabited wing of Stoke Moran Manor House
text: From the upper floor of the Crown they can see both the gate and the inhabited wing.

reads: At dusk we saw Dr. Grimesby Roylott drive past
text: Roylott comes home at dusk.
He is back by evening, as Helen expected. The visit to the rooms stayed clear of him.

reads: we heard the hoarse roar of the Doctor’s voice and saw the fury with which he shook his clinched fists at him
text: He arrives in a rage over a gate, and he knows Helen went to Holmes. This is the homecoming Holmes feared for her, and now the headache pretence has to protect her.

reads: we saw a sudden light spring up among the trees as the lamp was lit in one of the sitting-rooms
text: The sitting-rooms are in the central block (¶33), so this lamp is not the signal. For the moment it suggests the household is up and away from the bedroom wing.
He has been away nearly all day, and we still hear nothing of the 'most important business' or of anything he brought back.
An ordinary household bed stands free on the floor and can be shifted by the people who use it.
exceptions: Beds on ships or in some institutions are fixed, and a very heavy bed may in practice stay where it is.

reads: There is a distinct element of danger.
text: He told Helen they would investigate 'this noise'. To Watson he speaks of danger, so the milder phrase was for her benefit.
What could endanger two men, one of them armed, waiting in that room?
options: Roylott himself, if he discovers them

reads: No, but I fancy that I may have deduced a little more. I imagine that you saw all that I did.
text: Holmes says the difference lies in reasoning and not in what was seen. If Watson saw it all, the reader should have most of it too, so the answer ought to be available from the room as described.

reads: It was so small that a rat could hardly pass through.
text: By Watson's estimate, the ventilator opening is smaller than a rat could comfortably use.

No person comes through this, so Julia may indeed have been alone. Nor does a cat-sized animal. If anything alive uses the opening it must be very thin, which leaves the long-bodied option on my list and hurts the small-mammal one. Watson's 'rat' is only a rough figure.
hindsight: Only a reader already considering a creature would measure the opening against one. Watson offers the size as a reason for thinking it harmless.

reads: I knew that we should find a ventilator before ever we came to Stoke Moran.
text: He claims to have got it from Helen's statement alone. So the clue was in the Baker Street account, and that account deserves going back over.

reads: that suggested at once that there must be a communication between the two rooms
text: The passing detail about the cigars is his starting point, and he confirms that the opening joins Julia's room to Roylott's. That also settles where the other end lies, which nobody had reported.

reads: I deduced a ventilator.
text: That is more than the cigars could establish. Smoke might have come by the corridor or the windows. It was a good guess that the visit happened to confirm.

reads: It could only be a small one, or it would have been remarked upon at the coroner’s inquiry.
text: Holmes also takes it that the inquiry passed over the opening. The 'sealed' room was sealed only against things large enough to be noticed.

reads: A ventilator is made, a cord is hung, and a lady who sleeps in the bed dies.
text: Holmes puts these in a sequence, fittings first and death after. Helen said only 'a couple of years ago' and 'about that time', so the order is his reading unless he has more. It is what the design theory requires, and nothing contradicts it.

reads: It was clamped to the floor.
text: Julia's bed is fastened to the floor.
Nobody needs to clamp a bedroom bed. Together with the dead bell and the false ventilator, that makes three things in this room that are not as they should be.
This is what he was staring at, and it fits my question about the other 'little changes', though no one has said when the clamps went on.

Going back: the description of the room gives the bed's place in a corner and its white counterpane, and ¶148 has Holmes staring at it. The clamps were never mentioned. This fact is new to the reader, whatever Holmes says about Watson having seen everything.

reads: It must always be in the same relative position to the ventilator and to the rope
text: The opening, the rope and the bed are locked into one arrangement. The tassel lies on the pillow, so the rope's lower end is always where the sleeper's head is.

reads: since it was clearly never meant for a bell-pull
text: The bed need be fixed only if something arrives at a particular spot. A mere excuse for workmen would not call for clamps, and neither would a gas. Of my options for the rope, 'something passes along it' now leads.

The rope itself is not the 'band'. It had hung in plain sight for some time, and she would not scream at a familiar fitting or need a new name for it. It looks like the route, and what she saw would be whatever came along it.
What goes from a tiny opening down a cord to a fixed pillow?
options: A thin living creature that climbs down the rope
A liquid poison run down the cord to the sleeper
Something let down on a line and drawn back
hindsight: Holmes has named nothing that travels. The creature option requires the reader to join the milk, the looped lash and the Indian animals unaided.

reads: I seem to see dimly what you are hinting at.
text: Watson claims a dim idea and does not state it. The reader gets the tension and no new fact.
William Palmer and Edward Pritchard were British doctors hanged in the mid-nineteenth century for murder by poison.
exceptions: The names were notorious in the period, and a later reader may not know them.

reads: When a doctor does go wrong he is the first of criminals.
text: He now says outright that the clever criminal is the doctor. Roylott is the man he means.

reads: Palmer and Pritchard were among the heads of their profession.
text: Both names mean poisoning doctors. Holmes's comparison turns the mind to poison, and to medical knowledge used quietly.

reads: This man strikes even deeper
text: The doctors looked for poison and found none (¶58). A doctor would know what they would look for and what they would miss. That may fill the gap I left in the creature idea.
options: A poison that country doctors would not recognise or test for
Something that is not a poison in the ordinary sense
The comparison is only about boldness and says nothing of the method
hindsight: Holmes names no method. Connecting this remark to an exotic poison depends on the reader's own creature hypothesis and on knowing that a venom could escape detection.

reads: But we shall have horrors enough before the night is over
text: He is sure that the attempt will come tonight, and that it will be ugly.

reads: About nine o’clock the light among the trees was extinguished
text: The sitting-room light goes out at about nine.

reads: just at the stroke of eleven, a single bright light shone out right in front of us
text: At eleven exactly a bright light appears facing the inn.
If this is the signal, Helen got through the evening well enough to carry out her instructions, and she has heard Roylott retire. Her shutters are now open and she is going to her old room.

Two hours lie between the sitting-room going dark and the signal. He may have sat up in his own room in the meantime, as he did on the night Julia died (¶35). If the whistle keeps to about three (¶40), there are some four hours to wait.

reads: it comes from the middle window
text: It is the right window, so the plan is going as arranged.

reads: explaining that we were going on a late visit to an acquaintance
text: The same care he took with the driver. Two guests going out at eleven and leaving their beds empty would cause talk, and this inn has already served Helen.

Open: what travels from the opening down the rope, what the 'speckled band' was, how something could kill and leave no trace for the doctors, what whistles and what clanged, what the milk, chair seat and looped lash mean, what is really in the safe, how Roylott traced Helen, and what his business in town was.

Working picture: Roylott, using a doctor's knowledge, built a fixed route from his room through a tiny opening and down a false bell-rope to a clamped bed, and Julia died at the end of it. Something very thin or fluid uses that route. Tonight Holmes and Watson wait in the bed's room while Helen is one door along. She probably survives, and Roylott's advertised death may come out of this night.
options: A thin creature sent through the opening and down the rope
A poison the doctors could not detect, delivered down the cord
Something else that has not yet been thought of
hindsight: Holmes has established the route and said nothing of what uses it. The creature option remains the reader's own construction from the milk, the lash and the Indian animals.
